claim: Live imaging showed that lack of ecdysone did not slow neuroblast cell cycle times.
source: Fourth, we used live imaging to directly measure cell cycle times and found that lack of ecdysone did not slow neuroblast cell cycle times.
evidence: This is evidence against a general developmental delay in the absence of ecdysone.

claim: Ecdysone signaling acts directly on larval neuroblasts to promote an early-to-late gene expression transition.
source: Taken together, these data support our conclusion that ecdysone signaling acts directly on larval neuroblasts to promote an early-to-late gene expression transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the study.

claim: The role of ecdysone in regulating developmental transitions during larval stages has been well studied.
source: The role of ecdysone in regulating developmental transitions during larval stages has been well studied; it can induce activation or repression of suites of genes in a concentration dependent manner (reviewed in Thummel, 2001; Yamanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Ecdysone induces changes through a heteromeric complex of EcR and the retinoid X receptor homolog Ultraspiracle.
source: Ecdysone induces these changes through a heteromeric complex of EcR and the retinoid X receptor homolog Ultraspiracle (King-Jones and Thummel, 2005; Yamanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ecdysone is required for termination of neuroblast proliferation at the larval/pupal transition.
source: Ecdysone is required for termination of neuroblast proliferation at the larval/pupal transition (Homem et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Ecdysone is known to play a significant role in remodeling of mushroom body neurons and at neuromuscular junctions.
source: and is known to play a significant role in remodeling of mushroom body neurons and at neuromuscular junctions (Awasaki and Lee, 2011; Kucherenko and Shcherbata, 2013; Lee et al., 2000; Schubiger et al., 1998; Yu and Schuldiner, 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ecdysone signaling triggers a major gene expression transition in mid-larval brain neuroblasts.
source: Here we add to this list another function: to trigger a major gene expression transition in mid-larval brain neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Syncrip can be detected in many neuroblasts by 60 hr.
source: For example, Syncrip can be detected in many neuroblasts by 60 hr
evidence: This is a description of the temporal expression pattern observed in the data.

claim: Broad appears slightly later at ~72 hr.
source: whereas Broad appears slightly later at ~72 hr
evidence: This is a description of the temporal expression pattern observed in the data.

claim: E93 is only detected much later at ~96 hr, by which time Broad is low.
source: and E93 is only detected much later at ~96 hr, by which time Broad is low
evidence: This is a description of the temporal expression pattern observed in the data.

claim: This staggered expression of ecdysone target genes is reminiscent of early and late ecdysone-inducible genes in other tissues.
source: This staggered expression of ecdysone target genes is reminiscent of early and late ecdysone-inducible genes in other tissues (Baehrecke, 1996).
evidence: This is a comparison to known patterns in other tissues, supported by a citation.

claim: The Hunchback-Krüppel-Pdm-Castor temporal gene transitions within embryonic neuroblasts are regulated by neuroblast-intrinsic mechanisms.
source: We have previously shown that the Hunchback-Krüppel-Pdm-Castor temporal gene transitions within embryonic neuroblasts are regulated by neuroblast-intrinsic mechanisms: they can occur normally in neuroblasts isolated in culture, and the last three factors are sequentially expressed in G2-arrested neuroblasts (Grosskortenhaus et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Optic lobe neuroblasts are likely to undergo neuroblast-intrinsic temporal transcription factor transitions.
source: Similarly, optic lobe neuroblasts are likely to undergo neuroblast-intrinsic temporal transcription factor transitions, based on the observation that these neuroblasts form over many hours of development and undergo their temporal transitions asynchronously (Bertet et al., 2014; Hasegawa et al., 2011; Li et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations cited from previous work.

claim: Ecdysone signaling triggers a mid-larval transition in gene expression in all central brain neuroblasts (both type I and type II).
source: In contrast, we show here that ecdysone signaling triggers a mid-larval transition in gene expression in all central brain neuroblasts (both type I and type II).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Ecdysone is present at all larval stages.
source: Although ecdysone is present at all larval stages
evidence: This is a statement about ecdysone levels, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Ecdysone triggers central brain gene expression changes only following Svp-dependent expression of EcR-B1 in neuroblasts.
source: it triggers central brain gene expression changes only following Svp-dependent expression of EcR-B1 in neuroblasts
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Precocious expression of EcR-B1 did not result in premature activation of the late factor Broad, despite the forced expression of high EcR-B1 levels in young neuroblasts.
source: Interestingly, precocious expression of EcR-B1 (worniu-gal4 UAS-EcR-B1) did not result in premature activation of the late factor Broad, despite the forced expression of high EcR-B1 levels in young neuroblasts (data not shown).
evidence: This is a description of an experimental result.

claim: There may be another required factor that is also temporally expressed at 56 hr.
source: Perhaps there is another required factor that is also temporally expressed at 56 hr.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that precocious EcR-B1 is not sufficient.

claim: Reduced ecdysone signaling in ecdts mutants or following EcRDN expression does not permanently block the Chinmo/Imp to Broad/Syncrip/E93 transition.
source: We also note that reduced ecdysone signaling in ecdts mutants or following EcRDN expression does not permanently block the Chinmo/Imp to Broad/Syncrip/E93 transition; it occurs with variable expressivity at 120–160 hr animals (pupariation is significantly delayed in these ecdts mutants)
evidence: This is a description of an observation from the experiments.

claim: The delayed transition in ecdysone-reduced conditions is either due to a failure to completely eliminate ecdysone signaling or the presence of an ecdysone-independent mechanism.
source: either due to a failure to completely eliminate ecdysone signaling or the presence of an ecdysone-independent mechanism
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the delayed transition.

claim: There is a small but reproducible difference in the effect of reducing ecdysone levels using the biosynthetic pathway mutant ecdts versus expressing a dominant negative EcR in type II neuroblasts.
source: We find a small but reproducible difference in the effect of reducing ecdysone levels using the biosynthetic pathway mutant ecdts versus expressing a dominant negative EcR in type II neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a description of an observation from the experiments.

claim: The ecdts genotype shows a highly penetrant failure to activate Broad in old neuroblasts.
source: The former genotype shows a highly penetrant failure to activate Broad in old neuroblasts
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype observed in ecdts mutants.

claim: The EcRDN genotype has normal expression of Broad (despite failure to down-regulate Chinmo/Imp or activate E93).
source: whereas the latter genotype has normal expression of Broad (despite failure to down-regulate Chinmo/Imp or activate E93)
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype observed in EcRDN-expressing neuroblasts.

claim: The difference between ecdts and EcRDN may be due to failure of the dominant negative protein to properly repress the Broad gene.
source: This may be due to failure of the dominant negative protein to properly repress the Broad gene.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the difference.

claim: Differences between EcRDN and other methods of reducing ecdysone signaling have been noted before.
source: Differences between EcRDN and other methods of reducing ecdysone signaling have been noted before (Brown et al., 2006; Homem et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Drosophila Svp is an orphan nuclear hormone receptor.
source: Drosophila Svp is an orphan nuclear hormone receptor (Mlodzik et al., 1990)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Svp has an evolutionarily conserved role in promoting a switch between temporal identity factors.
source: with an evolutionarily conserved role in promoting a switch between temporal identity factors (Kohwi and Doe, 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: In Drosophila, Svp is required to switch off hunchback expression in embryonic neuroblasts.
source: In Drosophila, Svp it is required to switch off hunchback expression in embryonic neuroblasts (Benito-Sipos et al., 2011; Kanai et al., 2005; Mettler et al., 2006)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In mammals the related COUP-TF1/2 factors are required to terminate early-born cortical neuron production.
source: and in mammals the related COUP-TF1/2 factors are required to terminate early-born cortical neuron production (Naka et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: COUP-TF1/2 factors are required for the neurogenic to gliogenic switch.
source: as well as for the neurogenic to gliogenic switch (Barnabé-Heider et al., 2005; reviewed in Kohwi and Doe, 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and a review article.

claim: Svp is required for activating expression of EcR, which drives the mid-larval switch in gene expression from Chinmo/Imp to Syncrip/Broad/E93 in central brain neuroblasts.
source: Here we show that Svp is required for activating expression of EcR, which drives the mid-larval switch in gene expression from Chinmo/Imp to Syncrip/Broad/E93 in central brain neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: The results are supported by independent findings that svp mutant clones lack expression of Syncrip and Broad in old type II neuroblasts.
source: Our results are supported by independent findings that svp mutant clones lack expression of Syncrip and Broad in old type II neuroblasts (T. Lee, personal communication).
evidence: This statement is based on personal communication.

claim: Svp is required for neuroblast cell cycle exit at pupal stages.
source: Interestingly, Svp is required for neuroblast cell cycle exit at pupal stages (Maurange et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Svp activates expression of EcR-B1, which is required for the expression of multiple late temporal factors in larval neuroblasts.
source: Our results provide a satisfying link between these findings: we show that Svp activates expression of EcR-B1, which is required for the expression of multiple late temporal factors in larval neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding and its implications.

claim: Any one of the late temporal factors could terminate neuroblast proliferation at pupal stages.
source: Any one of these factors could terminate neuroblast proliferation at pupal stages
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of cell cycle exit.

claim: One orphan nuclear hormone receptor (Svp) activates expression of a second nuclear hormone receptor (EcR) in neuroblasts.
source: It is interesting that one orphan nuclear hormone receptor (Svp) activates expression of a second nuclear hormone receptor (EcR) in neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a summary of the regulatory relationship discovered in the study.

claim: This motif of nuclear hormone receptors regulating each other is widely used in Drosophila, C. elegans, and vertebrates.
source: This motif of nuclear hormone receptors regulating each other is widely used in Drosophila, C. elegans, and vertebrates (Boulanger et al., 2011; Faunes and Larraín, 2016; Gissendanner et al., 2004; Lam et al., 1999; Thummel, 2001; Yamanaka et al., 2013; Zelhof et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The position of the Svp+ neuroblasts varied among the type II neuroblast population from brain-to-brain.
source: The position of the Svp+ neuroblasts varied among the type II neuroblast population from brain-to-brain
evidence: This is a description of the observed expression pattern.

claim: Svp may be expressed in all type II neuroblasts but in a transient, asynchronous manner.
source: suggesting that Svp may be expressed in all type II neuroblasts but in a transient, asynchronous manner
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed expression pattern.

claim: The svp-lacZ transgene, which encodes a long-lived β-galactosidase protein, can be detected in nearly all type II neuroblasts.
source: This conclusion is supported by two findings: the svp-lacZ transgene, which encodes a long-lived β-galactosidase protein, can be detected in nearly all type II neuroblasts
evidence: This is a description of the reporter expression data.

claim: Svp is required for EcR expression in all type II neuroblasts, consistent with transient Svp expression in all type II neuroblasts.
source: and our finding that Svp is required for EcR expression in all type II neuroblasts, consistent with transient Svp expression in all type II neuroblasts
evidence: This is an inference based on the svp mutant clone data.

claim: Asynchronous expression of Svp is more consistent with a neuroblast-intrinsic cue, perhaps linked to the time of quiescent neuroblast re-activation, than with a lineage-extrinsic cue.
source: It is unknown what activates Svp in type II neuroblasts; its asynchronous expression is more consistent with a neuroblast-intrinsic cue, perhaps linked to the time of quiescent neuroblast re-activation, than with a lineage-extrinsic cue.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of Svp activation.

claim: Castor and its vertebrate homolog Cas-Z1 specify temporal identity in Drosophila embryonic neuroblast lineages and vertebrate retinal progenitor lineages, respectively.
source: Castor and its vertebrate homolog Cas-Z1 specify temporal identity in Drosophila embryonic neuroblast lineages and vertebrate retinal progenitor lineages, respectively (Grosskortenhaus et al., 2006; Mattar et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cas is not required for the Chinmo/Imp to Syncrip/Broad/E93 transition.
source: Although we show here that Cas is not required for the Chinmo/Imp to Syncrip/Broad/E93 transition, it has other functions.
evidence: This is a summary of the finding from the cas mutant analysis.

claim: Cas expression in larval neuroblasts is required to establish a temporal Hedgehog gradient that ultimately triggers neuroblast cell cycle exit at pupal stages.
source: Cas expression in larval neuroblasts is required to establish a temporal Hedgehog gradient that ultimately triggers neuroblast cell cycle exit at pupal stages (Chai et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Drosophila embryonic neuroblasts change gene expression rapidly, often producing just one progeny in each temporal transcription factor window.
source: Drosophila embryonic neuroblasts change gene expression rapidly, often producing just one progeny in each temporal transcription factor window (Baumgardt et al., 2009; Isshiki et al., 2001; Moris-Sanz et al., 2014; Novotny et al., 2002; Pearson and Doe, 2003; Tran and Doe, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Larval neuroblasts divide ~50 times over their 120 hr lineage.
source: In contrast, larval neuroblasts divide ~50 times over their 120 hr lineage (Truman and Bate, 1988; Yu and Lee, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mushroom body neuroblasts make just four different neuronal classes over time.
source: Mushroom body neuroblasts make just four different neuronal classes over time (Ito and Awasaki, 2008; Liu et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2006)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The AD (ALad1) neuroblast makes ~40 distinct projection neuron subtypes.
source: whereas the AD (ALad1) neuroblast makes ~40 distinct projection neuron subtypes (Kao et al., 2012; Lai et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Larval type II neuroblasts undergo at least seven molecularly distinct temporal windows.
source: Here we find that larval type II neuroblasts undergo at least seven molecularly distinct temporal windows (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings, illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: If the graded expression of Imp (high early) and Syncrip (high late) can specify fates in a concentration-dependent manner, many more temporal windows could exist.
source: If we assume that the graded expression of Imp (high early) and Syncrip (high late) can specify fates in a concentration-dependent manner, many more temporal windows could exist.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential for additional temporal windows.

claim: All of the factors characterized respond to ecdysone signaling in an all-or-none manner, with the exception of Syncrip.
source: All of the factors characterized here respond to ecdysone signaling in an all-or-none manner, with the exception of Syncrip.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings regarding ecdysone responsiveness.

claim: Loss of ecdysone signaling in the ecdts mutant results in persistent expression of the early factors Chinmo and Imp, and loss of expression of the late factors Broad and E93, in all central brain neuroblasts.
source: For example, loss of ecdysone signaling in the ecdts mutant results in persistent expression of the early factors Chinmo and Imp, and loss of expression of the late factors Broad and E93, in all central brain neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the ecdts mutant analysis.

claim: Syncrip is only partially reduced by loss of ecdysone signaling.
source: In contrast, Syncrip is only partially reduced by loss of ecdysone signaling
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype observed for Syncrip in ecdysone mutants.

claim: There is at least one additional input that drives Syncrip expression.
source: suggesting that there is at least one additional input that drives Syncrip expression
evidence: This is an inference based on the partial reduction of Syncrip in ecdysone mutants.

claim: Imp RNAi has been shown to modestly increase syncrip levels in the MB neuroblasts.
source: Imp RNAi has been shown to modestly increase syncrip levels in the MB neuroblasts (Liu et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Imp RNAi does not de-repress Syncrip in 24 hr type II neuroblasts.
source: but does not de-repress Syncrip in 24 hr type II neuroblasts (T. Lee, personal communication)
evidence: This statement is based on personal communication.

claim: Imp mutants do not show an increase in the number of Syncrip+ type II neuroblasts at 48 hr.
source: We find that Imp mutants do not show an increase in the number of Syncrip+ type II neuroblasts at 48 hr
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype observed in Imp mutants.

claim: The level of Syncrip protein following imp RNAi is elevated at 48 hr.
source: although the level of Syncrip protein following imp RNAi is elevated at 48 hr (T. Lee, personal communication)
evidence: This statement is based on personal communication.

claim: Syncrip repression of Imp seems to be robust and conserved among all neuroblast populations tested to date.
source: Although Imp repression of Syncrip may vary in penetrance and among different types of neuroblasts, Syncrip repression of Imp seems to be robust and conserved among all neuroblast populations tested to date (Liu et al., 2015; this work).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the current study and previous work.
